Technology and innovation in the study of food choice behavior
Computerized tools can extend the assessment of food choice beyond the laboratory. Tools such as the Web Buffet (Bucher et al.,
2012), the Food Choice Task (Foerde et al., 2018; Masterson et al., 2019; Hare et al., 2009), or the Multiple Food Test (Schreiber
et al., 2020) provide participants with a variety of food choice situations. These paradigms allow for multiple comparisons to be
made within a short period of time. Additionally, speciﬁc food comparisons (e.g., low-vs. high-energy dense foods) can be tested
to better understand the sensory and nutritional characteristics that drive food choice. An advantage of these online tools is that they
can be administered to large numbers of participants at a low cost. Such large-scale data collection can aid in the identiﬁcation of
individual variability related to food choice (e.g., (Brodock et al., 2021), and this could be used to develop tailored interventions to
improve dietary intake.
One method originally developed by addiction researchers to study behavior in a participant’s usual environment, Ecological
Momentary Assessment (EMA), has promise for the study of food choice. Broadly, EMA allows intensive data collection about
a participant’s behavior to be collected in real time during their daily routine (Shiffman et al., 2008). The evaluation of real-
world food choices via EMA helps to minimize recall and response biases (Shiffman et al., 2008). Further, computerized food choice
